reels.title: Promises the platform makes

beats.say: Forty teams depend on the data platform. What does it promise them?
A service level indicator measures something users feel, as a share of good events: loads on time, jobs that succeed, queries that are fast.
A service level objective is the target for that share over a window, such as ninety-nine and a half percent of loads on time over thirty days.
Publish the promises and how you are doing against them, where every team can see them.

check.q: Which is a good service level indicator for a data platform?
opts: The share of loads that land on time
The number of tables in the catalog
The number of engineers on call
check.why: Indicators measure what users feel, as a share of good events.

work: Write two indicators users of your platform feel.
Set a 30-day target for each.

reels.title: The error budget

beats.say: Ninety-nine and a half percent on time. What about the other half percent?
The error budget is what the objective allows to fail: half a percent of loads. While budget is left, the team ships features. When it is spent, reliability comes first.
Agree the policy with leadership before an incident, not during one. Then nobody argues when the budget runs out.
An error budget makes reliability a shared, measured decision, not a mood.

check.q: The error budget for the month is spent. What does the policy say?
opts: Pause features and fix reliability first
Raise the target so the budget grows
Ignore it until next month starts
check.why: The agreed policy trades feature work for reliability when users are hurt.

work: Write your platform's error budget policy in three lines.
Get your manager to agree to it before the next incident.

reels.title: Burn-rate alerts

beats.say: Should every failed job page someone at night?
Burn rate is how fast the budget is being used. A burn rate of one spends it exactly over the window. Seven percent errors against a half percent budget is a burn rate of fourteen point four.
Page when the last hour burns at about fourteen. Open a ticket when the last six hours burn at about six. Ignore blips that do neither.
Fewer, better pages mean people trust the pager again.

check.q: The SLO allows 0.5% errors and the last hour had 7.2% errors. What is the burn rate?
check.why: 7.2% divided by 0.5% is 14.4, fast enough to page.

work: Compute last week's burn rate for one SLO.
Replace one noisy alert with a burn-rate alert.

reels.title: Service levels in a staff interview

beats.say: Interview question: which service levels would you set for a data platform?
Ingestion freshness, job success, interactive query latency and availability of core services, each as a share of good events over thirty days.
Then say how you use them: an error budget policy agreed with leadership, burn-rate alerts instead of noise, and attainment shown on a page every team can read.
Interviewers listen for what happens when the budget runs out. Say it.

check.q: What do interviewers listen for after you list the SLOs?
opts: What happens when the error budget runs out
How many dashboards the team has built
Which vendor provides the monitoring tool
check.why: The policy shows the SLOs actually change decisions.

work: Practise the one-minute answer out loud.
Add the policy sentence at the end.

reels.title: A platform is a product

beats.say: Is your data platform team a ticket desk that answers requests, or a product team with users and a plan?
A ticket desk does whatever arrives loudest and counts tickets closed. A product team knows its users, publishes service levels, has a roadmap and measures adoption.
Its users are domain engineers, analysts, ML engineers and data product owners, each with different jobs and pains.
Often it also needs a product manager, not only engineers.

check.q: What marks a platform run as a product rather than a ticket desk?
opts: Users, service levels, a roadmap and adoption
Closing the most tickets each week
Building whatever the loudest team asks
check.why: Product teams research users and measure outcomes.

work: List your platform's user types.
Write one pain each type has today.

reels.title: Knowing your users

beats.say: How do you find out what users of a platform need?
Interview five users of each type every quarter, shadow one journey end to end, read the support questions, and run a short survey.
Write down the top journeys with how long they take today and where they hurt. That list decides what to build next.
Users rarely ask for the thing that would help most. Watching them work shows it.

check.q: What is the best way to find a journey's real pain?
opts: Shadow a user doing it end to end
Ask only the most senior engineer
Count the tables they have created
check.why: Watching shows waits and workarounds people never mention.

work: Shadow one user through one journey this month.
Write down every wait you see.

reels.title: Cost showback

beats.say: The bill is four million a year. Who spends it?

show.sub: To the teams who spend it

beats.say: Showback shows each team what its data costs. Chargeback moves the money to their budget. Start with showback, so the numbers earn trust first.
You need tags on every resource, a fair key for shared costs, unit costs people can act on, and a monthly report per team.
Watch the untagged share. If a third of spend has no owner, nobody trusts the report.

check.q: Why start with showback before chargeback?
opts: It builds trust in the numbers first
It is required by every cloud provider
It is the only way to tag resources
check.why: Charging people for numbers they dispute damages trust.

work: Find your platform's untagged share of spend.
Pick one unit cost to report monthly.

reels.title: Measuring adoption and outcomes

beats.say: Tables created, tickets closed, petabytes stored. Are those good numbers?
Measure adoption, time from a new data product to its first consumer query, delivery metrics, service level attainment, satisfaction and unit costs.
Look at funnels too. Of the teams that signed up, how many shipped a product, ran it in production, and use it weekly? The biggest drop is your next project.
Report the same few numbers every month, so the trend tells the story.

check.q: Which number best shows a platform delivers value?
opts: Days from a new product to its first query
The number of tables created this year
The petabytes stored on the platform
check.why: Time to value measures what users get; the others count activity.

work: Draw your platform's adoption funnel.
Name the step with the biggest drop.

reels.title: On-call and incidents

beats.say: When the shared platform breaks, every team that depends on it is hit at the same moment.
Use a rotation with a runbook per alert. Name an incident lead, fixers, and someone who communicates.
Keep a status page, so teams look in one place instead of asking in ten channels. After serious incidents, write a blameless review with owners and dates.
Track how often users find incidents before the platform team does. That number should fall.

check.q: Why keep a status page for the platform?
opts: Teams look in one place, not ten channels
It replaces the need for any on-call rota
Auditors require one for every service
check.why: One source of truth cuts noise and repeated questions.

work: Set up a simple status page for your platform.
Count incidents users found first last month.

reels.title: The roadmap and saying no

beats.say: Sixty requests arrive every quarter, and the team has room for about fifteen of them. How do you choose?
Collect requests in one intake. Score them openly, for example reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort.
Reserve capacity: most for the roadmap, some for reliability and debt, some for support. Give reliability more when the error budget is low.
Say no clearly, with the reason and a workaround. Saying yes to everything delivers nothing well.

check.q: Two requests: 10 teams, impact 2, confidence 0.8, effort 4; or 3 teams, impact 3, confidence 1, effort 1. Which ranks higher?
opts: The second, scoring 9 against 4
The first, because it reaches more teams
They tie because both are worth doing

work: Score your top ten requests with RICE.
Publish what is not planned, and why.

reels.title: Is the platform worth its cost?

beats.say: The CTO asks what four million a year buys.
Show costs and outcomes together: spend with unit costs, teams and products on the platform, time to value before and after, service levels, and satisfaction.
Compare with the alternative: every team running its own stack. Then name next quarter's bets, the outcome each should move, and what you stopped doing.
One page, the same numbers every month. Leadership trusts trends, not one good slide.

check.q: What should you compare the platform's cost against?
opts: Each team running its own stack
Last year's number of tickets closed
The salary of the platform team's lead
check.why: The real alternative is many teams paying for their own stacks and people.

work: Draft the monthly one-pager for your platform.
Estimate the cost of teams running their own stacks.

reels.title: Teams are leaving the platform

beats.say: Three teams have started building their own stacks around the platform. What now?
Talk to them first. Usually the platform is unreliable, slow to start with, or missing something they need.
Fix reliability with service levels and an error budget policy, put their needs on the roadmap, and make the platform the fastest way to do the common journeys.
Keep the guardrails required for everyone, on the platform or not. Earn the rest.

check.q: Teams are building their own stacks. What do you do first?
opts: Ask them what the platform failed to give
Forbid any stack outside the platform
Cut their budgets until they come back
check.why: Their reasons tell you what to fix; mandates breed workarounds.

work: Interview one team that built its own stack.
Put their top need on the roadmap.
